title: English ‘foot’ and Latin ‘pēs’ grew from the same ancient word
body: Latin and English both descend from Proto-Indo-European, a language nobody wrote down, so its words are rebuilt by comparison and marked with an asterisk: ∗pṓds, ‘foot’. In the first millennium BCE the ancestor of the Germanic languages shifted its stops in a chain: p, t, k became f, þ (th) and h; b, d, g became p, t, k; and the aspirated bʰ, dʰ, gʰ became b, d, g. Rasmus Rask found the pattern and Jacob Grimm set it out in 1822, which is why Latin pēs, trēs and decem line up with foot, three and ten.

slides.heading: Match the Latin word to its English cousin
slides.explanation: p became f, t became þ (th), d became t, g became k and k became h: the regular shifts of Grimm’s law.

slides.alt: Animation in a philologist’s notebook: Latin pēs, trēs, canis, decem beside English foot, three, hound, ten; the starred ancestor *pṓds; a grid in which p, t, k slide to f, þ, h, then b, d, g to p, t, k, and bʰ, dʰ, gʰ to b, d, g, like links in a chain; then Rask, Grimm and Verner.
slides.music: “Prelude in C (BWV 846)” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Pick each pair of cousins and watch the sound that moved. Can you see the chain?
slides.takeaway: In early Germanic p, t and k became f, þ and h; b, d and g became p, t and k; bʰ, dʰ and gʰ became b, d and g. Latin kept the older sounds, so pēs and foot, decem and ten are cousins.

slides.question: Why did ∗ph₂tḗr, ‘father’, become Proto-Germanic ∗fadēr, with d rather than þ?
options: The stress fell after that consonant
slides.explanation: Verner’s law: the fricative from Grimm’s law became voiced when the syllable before it was unstressed. In ∗bʰréh₂tēr the stress came first, so brother kept its þ.

slides.heading: Why it matters
slides.text: Grimm’s law was the first time scholars saw sound change as systematic rather than accidental. Regular laws let linguists rebuild lost words and tell true cousins from look-alikes.
